A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same GraphFM research, retaining the core architecture, pretraining corpus and node-classification benchmarks. Their main text, appendices, equations, tables and figures are readable and support comparison. Internal reporting inconsistencies do not prevent identifying the revisions.

before.justification: V1 reports original GraphFM classification results, model/data scaling experiments, hyperparameter sensitivity analyses and GPU-utilization measurements, including supplementary learning curves.

after.justification: V2 retains original GraphFM experiments and adds decoder fine-tuning results, domain and synthetic-data ablations, computational ablations and graph-classification experiments.

M1.justification: V2 adds NFT, which progressively unfreezes the node decoder with learning-rate decay, beyond v1's adaptation of dataset-specific input/output components. Appendix D.4 also introduces a trainable cross-attention graph decoder for graph-level prediction. These extend the adaptation procedure and outputs, while the core encoder configurations and distributed sampler remain unchanged.

E1.justification: The 152-dataset pretraining corpus and ten node-classification benchmarks are retained. V2 additionally evaluates graph-level classification on MUTAG and PROTEINS (Appendix D.4, Table A7), substantially extending task coverage beyond v1's node-level evaluations. The domain-stratified experiments reuse existing pretraining data.

E2.justification: V2 adds LINKX and NAGphormer to the heterophilic comparisons, fills previously missing comparator results, and adds GraphAny comparisons and graph-classification baselines including GT, SAT and SpecFormer. Most earlier baselines remain in Tables A8–A9 rather than being removed; the earlier heterophilic ET row is absent.

E3.justification: V2 introduces domain-stratified and real-only pretraining controls, NFT unfreezing-schedule tuning, mean-rank evaluation across ten benchmarks, and an 18M-parameter efficiency ablation. Existing node-benchmark split descriptions remain unchanged. V2 also describes MFT as feature-MLP-only, whereas v1 explicitly updates the output classifier too; whether this wording reflects an implementation change is unresolved.

E4.justification: V2 adds domain-composition and synthetic-data ablations, per-dataset scaling breakdowns, and sampler/packing removal experiments (Figure 4B and Appendices C–D). Learning-dynamics comparisons expand from GCN to NAGphormer. Existing sensitivity plots are retained and reorganized, although v1's separate Texas and Physics convergence plots are omitted.

E5.justification: V2 introduces between-dataset rank standard deviations and corresponding error bars in Figure 5 and Table A6, supplementing v1's split-level accuracy dispersion. No increased repeat count or new significance-testing procedure is established. Both versions retain the inconsistency between ten-split table captions and the homophilic appendix's twenty-random-split description.

E6.justification: V2 adds NFT, graph-classification, domain-ablation, ranking and efficiency results; Table A7 reports GraphFM accuracies of 93.8±6.6 on MUTAG and 76.4±3.7 on PROTEINS. Many original results persist, but the Texas MFT entry changes from 80.54±2.76 to 80.81±2.76. V2 inconsistently reports ogbn-arxiv MFT as 69.96±0.21 in Table A6 and 65.29±0.16 in Table A8, preventing an unambiguous same-setting improvement claim.

T1.justification: The stated node-decoder complexity changes from M(K+T+1)^2 in v1 Section 2.2 to Ng M(K+T+1)^2 in v2 Section 3.1.2, revising the computational accounting. No new theorem or proof is supplied; much of the added background mathematics explains existing attention and spectral encodings.

C1.justification: The central claims of scalable multi-domain pretraining, favorable scaling and stable competitive transfer remain. V2 adds explicit claims that NFT achieves the best mean rank across ten test graphs and MFT ranks second, distinguishing two adaptation regimes rather than v1's single frozen-backbone evaluation.

C2.justification: V2 interprets the new ablations as evidence for transfer from unrelated domains and for diversity beyond data size, and explains specialist rank variability. It qualifies unseen graphs as potentially structurally similar to training graphs, treats domain boundaries as practical choices, states the lack of edge-feature support, and distinguishes GraphAny's zero-shot setting from supervised fine-tuning. These substantially expand interpretation and applicability boundaries.

D1.justification: V2 adds a GraphFM code-location statement, previously unspecified training duration in epochs and batch size, exact pretraining subset lists, NFT unfreezing hyperparameters and additional resource accounting. These materially improve implementation documentation without establishing changes to the retained experiments. Conversely, Table A4 omits statistics for four fine-tuning datasets that appeared in v1 Table A3.

R1.justification: The related-work discussion expands substantially to GraphAny, GCOPE, MDGPT, GraphProp, GFSE and other foundation-model and scaling research. V1's positioning as the first approach spanning diverse domains shifts toward differentiation by pretraining scale and diversity among existing cross-domain approaches, beyond bibliographic or citation-style updates.

P1.justification: V2 extensively rewrites the abstract, introduction and conclusion, adds a background section, separates datasets from results, reorganizes methods and experimental questions, and restructures the appendices. The title, affiliations and publication headers also change. This is substantial narrative reorganization beyond inserting new experiments.

P2.justification: The original benchmark tables move to the appendix, with a new consolidated comparison table and ranking plots. Scaling Figure 4 gains a domain panel; sensitivity and convergence displays are separated and rearranged; the main GPU-utilization plot changes from violins to density curves. Additional ablation figures, graph-classification tables and extensive layout changes materially revise the presentation.

improvement.justification: The domain/synthetic-data and GPU ablations strengthen previously thin empirical support, while adaptation schedules, subset lists and a code link improve reproducibility. However, conflicting scores across Tables A6, A8 and A10, limited protocol details for graph classification, and blanket no-tuning language despite NFT schedule tuning undermine parts of the expanded evaluation. The added support provides a positive but limited net improvement.
